title: Presence & Attention

learn.summary: Compassion starts before any words: it requires actually noticing another person. Stanford's Compassion Cultivation Training (CCT) begins with attention-settling practices for exactly this reason — a distracted mind literally cannot register suffering. Attention is trainable, and giving someone your undivided attention is itself a form of care.

do: Pick one daily conversation this week (dinner, coffee, a call) and give it 100% attention — no phone in sight, no mental rehearsing of your reply.

children.title: Phone-Free Presence

learn.summary: Phubbing — snubbing a companion by looking at your phone — measurably lowers relationship satisfaction and the other person's sense of being valued, even when the phone is merely visible on the table. Presence is now a scarce gift; the mere-presence effect means the device does not need to buzz to divide you.

do: For the next 7 days, leave your phone in another room during every shared meal. Count the days you succeed.

children.title: Noticing Suffering

learn.summary: Compassion researchers define it as a four-step sequence: notice suffering, feel moved, wish for relief, act. Most failures of compassion are failures at step one — we walk past distress because we are busy, not because we are cruel (the classic Darley and Batson 'Good Samaritan' study showed hurried seminary students stepped over a slumped stranger). Slowing down is a moral act.

do: Once a day this week, scan the people around you and silently name one thing someone might be struggling with. Just notice — no action required yet.

children.title: Mindful Attention

learn.summary: CCT and Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR both open with breath-focused attention training because a settled mind is the platform for every later skill. The mechanics are simple: attend to the breath, notice when the mind wanders, return without self-criticism. The 'return' is the rep — wandering is not failure, it is the gym.

do: Do 5 minutes of breath-counting (count exhales 1–10, restart when lost) on 5 of the next 7 days.

children.title: Just Like Me

learn.summary: A signature CCT practice: looking at a stranger and silently noting 'just like me, this person has known loss; just like me, this person wants to be happy.' It converts abstract crowds into individuals and reliably softens judgment in seconds. It works precisely because it is embarrassingly simple.

do: In one queue or commute this week, pick three strangers and silently run the 'just like me' phrases for each.

reflect: When did you last give someone your full, undivided attention — and what changed in the conversation when you did?
